panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Grayscale ultrasound of left kidney showing a large renal mass with hypoechoic/necrotic components in a patient with Denys-Drash Syndrome, consistent with Wilms tumor. B: Color Doppler ultrasound of left kidney showing minimal internal vascularity in the renal mass, consistent with Wilms tumor in Denys-Drash Syndrome. C: Grayscale ultrasound of right kidney showing a large renal mass in a patient with Denys-Drash Syndrome, consistent with Wilms tumor. D: Color Doppler ultrasound of right kidney showing minimal internal vascularity in the renal mass, consistent with Wilms tumor in Denys-Drash Syndrome.

in_text_mentions: Initial renal ultrasound (Figure 4) revealed large bilateral lower pole masses with hypoechoic, likely necrotic centers and minimal internal vascularity. A contrast‐enhanced abdominal CT scan (Figure 5) confirmed the presence of a horseshoe kidney with bilateral heterogeneously enhancing lower pole masses.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Hematoxylin and eosin stained histology section of resected nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor), a hallmark malignancy of Denys-Drash syndrome. The image shows characteristic histopathological features of the tumor. B: Immunohistochemical staining for WT1 protein in resected nephroblastoma tissue from a Denys-Drash syndrome patient, demonstrating the characteristic genetic marker associated with this syndrome and its associated Wilms tumor.

in_text_mentions: The patient had proteinuria without microscopic hematuria. She underwent a renal biopsy and histopathological examination indicated a diagnosis of Wilms tumor, and then, a right nephrectomy was performed. The pathologic report revealed a nephroblastoma (mesenchymal type) with necrosis based on the National Wilms Tumor Study Group 5 (NWTS‐5) classification criteria (Figure 4). The normal renal tissue structure was clear and demonstrated no evidence of glomerulosclerosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Frontal abdominal radiograph from an infant with Denys-Drash syndrome demonstrating enlarged horseshoe kidney with soft tissue density and bowel displacement, consistent with the disease's associated congenital renal anomalies. B: Coronal contrast-enhanced CT from an infant with Denys-Drash syndrome showing horseshoe kidney with bilateral heterogeneous lower pole masses (Wilms tumors) and right hydronephrosis, representing a key malignancy associated with the syndrome.

panels.figure_caption: (A) Frontal abdomen radiograph shows central and superior displacement of the aerated bowel loops. Large soft tissue density is noted in the right and left abdomen, which is related to the enlarged horseshoe kidney. (B) An enhanced CT scan of the abdomen in coronal view shows bilateral renal enlargement with cross‐fusion of the lower renal poles, representing horseshoe kidney. Bilateral lower renal poles demonstrate large heterogeneous masses. Right hydronephrosis is also appreciated (Case 2).
in_text_mentions: Initial renal ultrasound (Figure 4) revealed large bilateral lower pole masses with hypoechoic, likely necrotic centers and minimal internal vascularity. Large soft tissue density is noted in the right and left abdomen, which is related to the enlarged horseshoe kidney. (B) An enhanced CT scan of the abdomen in coronal view shows bilateral renal enlargement with cross‐fusion of the lower renal poles, representing horseshoe kidney. Bilateral lower renal poles demonstrate large heterogeneous masses. Right hydronephrosis is also appreciated (Case 2).

panels.rationale: Real patient renal ultrasound from a confirmed Denys-Drash syndrome case (per article title and in-text workup description). The arrow highlights a hypoechoic renal lesion consistent with Wilms tumor, a recognized manifestation of Denys-Drash syndrome. The case is described as having an atypical, attenuated presentation of nephropathy, aligning with the atypical typicality rating.

in_text_mentions: included a biopsy of the left (solitary) kidney that revealed numerous sclerosing glomeruli likely related to chronic glomerular injury. Given his solitary kidney at presentation, CKD, and previous pathology report indicating glomerular disease, we chose not to pursue a renal biopsy because of the high risk involved and minimal degree of proteinuria. Instead, we performed genetic analysis, regular laboratory tests (serum albumin, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), eGFR, electrolytes, lipid profile, URPC, urinalysis, complete blood count (CBC), coagulation profile) and renal ultrasound (Figs. 2 and 3).
